the three-dimensional structure and the cyclic nature of MCoTI-I, a new macrocyclic protein from Momordica, is very similar to those of other plant cyclotides and trypsin inhibitors, and that this is probably due to the need to protect the protein from proteolytic degradation.
the three-dimensional structure and disulphide connectivity of the plant cyclotides have now been expanded to include the trypsin inhibitor MCoTI-II.
(a) the three-dimensional structure is very similar to those of known plant cyclic peptides, and (b) the cyclic backbone of MCoTI-I may be a means of protecting it against proteolysis.

understanding the structure and function of the plant cyclotides and the role they play in plant defence.
the design, synthesis and evaluation of new cyclic and linear peptides and proteins as potential therapeutic agents for the treatment of cancer.
the development of new methods for the synthesis of cyclic peptides, the discovery and characterization of new cyclic peptides and the application of cyclic peptides in medicine.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have discovered a new family of cyclic proteins, which we have termed the ‘cyclophilins’ (cyclic proteins), and have identified their role in the regulation of cell proliferation in plants.
the cyclotides are a family of plant proteins with a cyclic backbone, a head-to-tile disulphide linkage, and a cysteine-knot motif.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the cyclization process is not limited to a specific class of protein, and that the resulting circular proteins may be functionally diverse.
the cyclization of proteins can confer a number of advantages, such as increased stability and resistance to degradation.
